modules.comments:
Error-diffusion and ordered dithering, in one import. This module
re-exports what a typical application needs:

- `ditherImage`, which dithers an image in memory; `ditherRows`, which
  dithers a lazy stream of rows, each when it's needed; and
  `initDithering` with `ditherRow`, one row at a time from any source;
- the kernels `floydSteinberg`, `atkinson` and `jarvisJudiceNinke`, and
  `noDiffusion` for none;
- the quantizers `threshold`, `nearestLevel` with `evenRamp`, and
  `perChannel` for color; `nearestColor` with the palette presets;
  `bayer` and `ordered` for ordered dithering;
- the pixel types `RGB` and `RGBA`, and the types for signatures.

Import it qualified, as names like `threshold` or `c64` are short:

```purescript
import Puregrain as P

dithered = P.ditherImage P.floydSteinberg (P.threshold 128.0) image
```

The building blocks for your own variants (distance metrics, threshold
maps, custom quantizers) are in the modules they come from:
`Puregrain.Palette`, `Puregrain.Ordered`, `Puregrain.Quantize`,
`Puregrain.Pixel` and `Puregrain.Kernel`. Dithering with cells, as on
the screens of 8-bit machines, is in `Puregrain.Cells` and
`Puregrain.Machine.ZxSpectrum`, outside this module.
modules.name: Puregrain

declarations.comments:
An image being dithered one row at a time, for `ditherRow`: the
kernel, the quantizer, and the error waiting for the rows still to
come; `a` is the pixel type. Opaque.

An immutable value: keep and reuse one, for an undo, say. Dithering a
row from it again redoes that row's work, and no more.
declarations.title: Dithering

declarations.comments:
The state before the first row, for `ditherRow`.

- `Kernel`: where each pixel's error goes; `noDiffusion` for nowhere.
- `Quantize a`: picks each pixel's output value.

Computes nothing yet; the first row fixes the image's width.
declarations.title: initDithering

declarations.comments:
Dithers a lazy stream of rows.

- `a`, `Kernel` and `Quantize a`: as for `ditherImage`.
- `LL.List (Array a)`: the rows, top to bottom, all of the same length;
  the list may be endless.

Returns the dithered rows as a lazy list, the same rows as
`ditherImage`. Each row is read and dithered only when its result is
first needed, so only the rows in flight are in memory. At a row whose
length differs from the first row's, it stops with an error naming
the row; the rows before it have come out.
declarations.title: ditherRows

declarations.comments:
Dithers the next row.

- `Dithering a`: the state, from `initDithering` or the previous row.
- `Array a`: the row, as long as the first one.

Returns the dithered row and the state for the next one: the same rows
as `ditherImage`. `Left`, with a message naming the row, for a row of a
different length; the state passed in is untouched, so you can carry
on with a corrected row.
declarations.title: ditherRow

declarations.comments:
Dithers an image in memory.

- `a`: the pixel type, `Number` for gray, `RGB` or `RGBA`; any type
  with `Ring` and `Scalable` works.
- `Kernel`: where each pixel's error goes; `noDiffusion` for nowhere.
- `Quantize a`: picks each pixel's output value.
- `Array (Array a)`: the image, rows top to bottom, each left to right,
  all of the same length.

Returns the dithered image, all at once. Stops with an error naming a
row whose length differs from the first row's.
declarations.title: ditherImage

declarations.comments:
One neighbour that gets a share of a pixel's error.

- `dx`: columns to the right; negative to the left.
- `dy`: rows down.
- `weight`: the share of the error.
declarations.title: Offset

declarations.comments:
A checked list of neighbours. Build one with `fromOffsets`, or use a
ready-made one. Opaque, so every kernel `ditherImage` gets is valid.
declarations.title: Kernel
noDiffusion

declarations.comments:
Jarvis–Judice–Ninke (1976): 12 neighbours over the next 2 rows, for
the smoothest texture, at about 2.5 times Floyd–Steinberg's cost.
declarations.title: jarvisJudiceNinke

declarations.comments: Floyd–Steinberg (1976): 4 neighbours, the classic.
declarations.title: floydSteinberg

declarations.comments:
Atkinson (Apple, 1980s): 6 neighbours over the next 2 rows, each
getting 1/8, so only 3/4 of the error is passed on: crisper and
higher in contrast, at the cost of detail in dark and light tones.
declarations.title: atkinson

declarations.comments:
A threshold map: a grid of thresholds, each strictly between 0 and 1,
repeated across the image. Build one with `bayer` or
`compileThresholdMap`; opaque, so every map is checked: rectangular
and non-empty.
declarations.title: ThresholdMap

declarations.comments:
Ordered dithering over levels. For a value `v` between two
neighbouring levels `lo` < `hi`, it picks `hi` exactly when
`(v − lo) / (hi − lo)` is above the pixel's threshold, else `lo`.

- `ThresholdMap`: the thresholds, from `bayer` or
  `compileThresholdMap`.
- `NonEmptyArray Number`: the levels, in any order; with 0 and 255,
  classic 1-bit ordered dithering.

A value at a level stays that level; values beyond the lowest or
highest level snap to it, as accumulated error can push them there in
the hybrid with error diffusion. For color, lift it with `perChannel`,
which gives every channel the same position.
declarations.title: ordered

declarations.comments:
The Bayer threshold map.

- `Int`: the side, a power of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, …).

`Nothing` for any other side. The thresholds are `(rank + 0.5) / n²`
for side `n` (see `compileThresholdMap`). `bayer 1` is 0.5 everywhere:
`ordered` with it picks the nearer level, like `nearestLevel`.

```purescript
-- pure 1-bit ordered dithering with the 8 × 8 map
map (\m -> ditherImage noDiffusion (ordered m (evenRamp 2)) image) (bayer 8)
```
declarations.title: bayer

declarations.comments:
A quantizer that turns each pixel into the nearest palette color, all
three channels together, by `distance2`; on a tie, the earlier color.

- `NonEmptyArray RGB`: the palette, e.g. from
  `Puregrain.Palette.Presets`.

```purescript
ditherImage floydSteinberg (nearestColor websafe216) image
```
declarations.title: nearestColor

declarations.comments:
The ZX Spectrum's 15 distinct colors: its 8 (black, blue, red, magenta,
green, cyan, yellow, white) at normal brightness, then the 7 non-black
ones with BRIGHT (bright black is black). Normal is 0xD8 = 216, about
85% of bright, the common model: the real colors were never measured,
and many emulators use 0xD7 or 0xCD instead. This is the per-pixel
palette; for the real machine's 2 colors per 8×8 cell, see
`Puregrain.Machine.ZxSpectrum`.
Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZX_Spectrum_graphic_modes; values as
lospec.com/palette-list/zx-spectrum.
declarations.title: zxSpectrum

declarations.comments:
The 216 "web-safe" colors: every combination of 0, 51, 102, 153, 204
and 255 per channel (a 6×6×6 cube), `r` varying slowest, so it starts
at black and ends at white. Being a complete grid, its nearest color is
the nearest step in each channel separately — the same result as
`perChannel (nearestLevel (evenRamp 6))`.
declarations.title: websafe216

declarations.comments:
The 16-color IBM PC palette, CGA's "RGBI" colors in index order 0–15:
each channel 0x00 or 0xAA, plus an intensity bit adding 0x55, with the
IBM 5153 monitor's brown (color 6 is #AA5500, not dark yellow). Also
EGA's and VGA's defaults and the DOS text colors; the Linux console
uses the same values, in ANSI order. EGA's full 64 colors need no
preset: `perChannel (nearestLevel (evenRamp 4))`.
Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_Graphics_Adapter (RGBI palette).
declarations.title: cga16

declarations.comments:
The Commodore 64's 16 colors, in VIC-II index order: black, white, red,
cyan, purple, green, blue, yellow, orange, brown, light red, dark grey,
grey, light green, light blue, light grey. There's no official RGB
definition; these are Pepto's calculated PAL values (2001, gamma
corrected), the de facto reference.
Source: pepto.de/projects/colorvic/2001/
declarations.title: c64

declarations.comments:
Black, then white. With `nearestColor` it dithers a color image
straight down to pure black and white, choosing by RGB distance —
which isn't brightness: pure green is nearer to black.
declarations.title: blackWhite

declarations.comments:
xterm's 256 colors: `ansi16` (indices 0–15), a 6×6×6 cube (16–231,
index 16 + 36r + 6g + b, levels 0, 95, 135, 175, 215, 255), and 24
grays (232–255, 8 + 10i). 7 cube colors repeat `ansi16` ones, so 249
are distinct; `nearestColor` picks the earlier index of a pair. In a
real terminal the first 16 come from its theme.
Source: xterm's 256colres.pl.
declarations.title: ansi256

declarations.comments:
The 16 ANSI terminal colors as xterm's defaults, in index order: black,
red, green, yellow, blue, magenta, cyan, white, then the 8 bright ones.
ANSI names the colors but defines no RGB, and terminals differ; the
Linux console's values are `cga16`, in CGA order.
Source: xterm's XTerm-col.ad, matching the xterm column of
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code.
declarations.title: ansi16

children.comments:
Alpha too, like the other channels, as in the `Ring` and `Scalable`
instances.
children.title: <anonymous>

declarations.comments:
A color pixel with alpha: as `RGB`, plus `a`, which error diffusion
treats like the other channels.
declarations.title: RGBA

children.comments: Compared and shown like the record inside.
children.title: <anonymous>

children.comments:
Channel by channel, `mul` and `one` too, though error diffusion uses
only `add`, `zero` and `sub`.
children.title: <anonymous>

declarations.comments:
A color pixel: red, green and blue, each from 0 to 255 by convention.
Adds, subtracts and scales channel by channel, as error diffusion
needs.
declarations.title: RGB

declarations.comments:
A gray pixel: one channel, a plain `Number`, from 0 (black) to 255
(white) by convention.
declarations.title: Gray

children.comments:
A gray pixel is its one channel: `perChannel` on `Number` is the
quantizer itself.
children.title: <anonymous>

children.comments:
Alpha too, like the other channels, as in the `Ring` and `Scalable`
instances.
children.title: <anonymous>

declarations.comments:
A pixel type whose channels can be mapped one by one: what
`Puregrain.Quantize.perChannel` needs to run a one-channel quantizer
on every channel. Laws, as for any functor-like mapping:

```purescript
mapChannels identity == identity
mapChannels (f <<< g) == mapChannels f <<< mapChannels g
```
declarations.title: MapChannels

declarations.comments:
A pixel type that error diffusion can scale by a kernel's weights.
With `Ring`, for adding and subtracting error, it's what `ditherImage`
needs from a pixel type.
declarations.title: Scalable

declarations.comments:
A quantizer: picks a pixel's output value; `a` is the pixel type.
Build one with `quantize`, or `quantizeWith` when the decision depends
on the pixel's position; run one with `runQuantize`. Opaque, so its
representation can change without breaking anyone.

It gets the pixel's corrected value, with the error diffused into it
already added, and must be total: accumulated error pushes values
beyond the nominal range, below 0 or above 255, and the quantizer must
still return a sensible value. `ditherImage` diffuses the difference
between the corrected value and the output to the neighbours.
declarations.title: Quantize

declarations.comments:
Where the pixel being quantized sits: column `x` and row `y`, from 0
at the top-left. A record so it can grow, with a seed say, without
breaking quantizers: a helper that needs only some fields can take
`forall r. { x :: Int, y :: Int | r }`.
declarations.title: Context

declarations.comments:
The classic 1-bit quantizer: 0 (black) below the threshold, 255
(white) at or above it.

- `Number`: the threshold, usually 128.

`nearestLevel (evenRamp 2)` is the same with the cut fixed at 127.5.
declarations.title: threshold

declarations.comments:
Runs a quantizer.

- `Quantize a`: the quantizer.
- `Context`: the pixel's position.
- `a`: the corrected value.

Returns the output value.
declarations.title: runQuantize

declarations.comments:
A quantizer that also gets the pixel's position: ordered or noise
dithering, say, or a lookup in per-pixel data such as a mask.

- `Context -> a -> a`: from the position and the corrected value to
  the output value.

```purescript
-- 1-bit with the cut at 64 and 192 in a checkerboard
quantizeWith \{ x, y } v ->
  if v < (if (x + y) `mod` 2 == 0 then 64.0 else 192.0) then 0.0 else 255.0
```
declarations.title: quantizeWith

declarations.comments:
A quantizer that ignores the pixel's position, the common case.

- `a -> a`: from the corrected value to the output value.

```purescript
-- 1-bit with the cut at 100
quantize \v -> if v < 100.0 then 0.0 else 255.0
```
declarations.title: quantize

declarations.comments:
Runs a one-channel quantizer on every channel of a pixel,
independently, each with the pixel's position.

- `a`: the pixel type, with `MapChannels`: `Number`, `RGB` or `RGBA`.
- `Quantize Number`: the quantizer for one channel.

Dithering an RGB image this way gives exactly what dithering its three
channel planes separately would: a `Quantize Number` only ever sees
one channel, so it can't couple them. For a quantizer that looks at
the whole pixel, see `Puregrain.Palette.nearestColor`.

```purescript
-- 4 levels per channel
perChannel (nearestLevel (evenRamp 4)) :: Quantize RGB
```
declarations.title: perChannel

declarations.comments:
Snaps a value to the nearest of the given levels: the one-channel
sibling of `Puregrain.Palette.nearestColor`.

- `NonEmptyArray Number`: the levels, in any order; on an exact tie,
  the earlier wins.

Values below the lowest level snap to it, values above the highest to
that one.

```purescript
nearestLevel (evenRamp 4)   -- 0, 85, 170 or 255
```
declarations.title: nearestLevel

declarations.comments:
Evenly spaced levels from 0 to 255, both ends included, for
`nearestLevel`.

- `Int`: how many; 1 or less gives the single midpoint, 127.5.

`evenRamp 2 == [0.0, 255.0]`, `evenRamp 4 == [0.0, 85.0, 170.0, 255.0]`.
declarations.title: evenRamp

modules.comments:
Dithering with cells: the image is divided into cells of `width ×
height` pixels, and each cell may use only one or two colors, chosen
for it from a list of candidates. That's how the attribute cells of
8-bit home computers work, such as the ZX Spectrum's 8 × 8 cells with
an ink and a paper color (`Puregrain.Machine.ZxSpectrum`). A
`CellMode` holds the cell size and the candidates; a machine module
exports one per screen mode. How it works and which rule suits which
picture: [docs/machine-screens/](https://github.com/roman-mkh/puregrain/blob/master/docs/machine-screens/README.md).

The image is processed in bands, one row of cells at a time. In each
band:

1. Every cell gets the candidate that fits its original pixels best.
   A candidate's score is the sum, over the cell's pixels, of each
   pixel's squared distance (in r, g and b) to the nearest color the
   candidate can produce: the nearest point on the segment between its
   two colors, since dithering can mix any share of them, or its one
   color. The lowest score wins; on a tie, the earlier candidate. A
   middle gray, for example, fits black and white perfectly, blue and
   white poorly.
2. The band's rows are dithered: a `CellQuantizer` turns each pixel
   into one of its cell's colors, and the kernel passes the error on,
   across cell and band borders.

`ditherCells` works on an image in memory, `ditherBands` on a lazy
stream of rows, with the same result:

```purescript
-- error diffusion inside the cells
ditherCells floydSteinberg nearestInCell mode image

-- pure ordered dithering inside the cells, with a threshold map m
ditherCells noDiffusion (orderedInCell m) mode image
```

declarations.comments:
The size of a cell in pixels, for `CellMode`. A width or height below
1 counts as 1.
declarations.title: CellSize

declarations.comments:
The colors one cell may use: one color, or two that dithering mixes.
Build it with `singleColor` or `colorPair`. The order of two colors
doesn't change which cells choose them, nor what `nearestInCell`
gives; with `orderedInCell` it sets the pattern's direction.
declarations.title: CellPalette

declarations.comments: A cell palette of one color.
declarations.title: singleColor

declarations.comments:
A cell palette of two colors. The same color twice is a single color.

- `RGB`: the first color.
- `RGB`: the second color; the order matters only for
  `orderedInCell`.
declarations.title: colorPair

declarations.comments: The palette's colors: one, or two in the order they were given.
declarations.title: cellColors

declarations.comments:
A screen mode for cells: how big a cell is, and which palettes a cell
may use. A machine module exports one per screen mode, such as
`Puregrain.Machine.ZxSpectrum.screen`.

- `c`: the candidate type, anything that stands for a cell's palette
  (for the ZX Spectrum, `Attribute`).
- `size`: the cell's width and height in pixels.
- `palette`: a candidate's colors.
- `candidates`: what a cell may use, in the order they're tried; on a
  tie the earlier wins.

For cells of your own, write the record; the candidates can be the
palettes themselves:

```purescript
mode :: CellMode CellPalette
mode =
  { size: { width: 4, height: 4 }
  , palette: identity
  , candidates: NEA.cons' (colorPair black white) [ colorPair blue yellow ]
  }
```

To change one part of a machine's mode, update its record, as in
`Zx.screen { candidates = fewer }`.
declarations.title: CellMode

declarations.comments:
How a pixel becomes one of its cell's colors. Build it with
`nearestInCell` or `orderedInCell`.
declarations.title: CellQuantizer

declarations.comments:
Each pixel becomes the nearer of its cell's colors, by squared RGB
distance (the first on a tie). With a kernel, that's error diffusion
inside the cells.
declarations.title: nearestInCell

declarations.comments:
Ordered dithering inside the cells. A pixel lies some fraction of the
way from its cell's first color to the second, measured along the
line between them; it becomes the second color where that fraction is
above the map's threshold at the pixel's position, else the first. A
single-color cell keeps its color.

- `ThresholdMap`: the thresholds, from `Puregrain.Ordered.bayer` or
  `compileThresholdMap`. Positions count from the image's corner, so
  any size works: a map whose side divides the cell's repeats in every
  cell, a larger one spreads more tone steps over several cells.

With `noDiffusion`, that's pure ordered dithering. With another kernel
it's the hybrid: the difference between a pixel's value and its color
is passed on.
declarations.title: orderedInCell

declarations.comments:
Dithers an image in memory with cells.

- `c`: the mode's candidate type (see `CellMode`).
- `Kernel`: where each pixel's error goes; `noDiffusion` for nowhere.
- `CellQuantizer`: how each pixel picks one of its cell's colors.
- `CellMode c`: the cell size, and the candidates with their colors.
- `Array (Array RGB)`: the image, rows top to bottom, all of the same
  length.

Returns the candidate chosen for each cell, as rows of cells (top to
bottom, each left to right), and the dithered image. An image whose
size isn't a multiple of the cell size gets partial cells at the
right and bottom edges. Stops with an error naming a row whose length
differs from the first row's.
declarations.title: ditherCells

declarations.comments:
Dithers a stream of rows with cells, one band (row of cells) at a
time.

- `c`, `Kernel`, `CellQuantizer` and `CellMode c`: as for `ditherCells`.
- `LL.List (Array RGB)`: the image as a lazy list of rows, top to
  bottom, all of the same length; it may be endless.

Returns a lazy list of bands, top to bottom, each with the candidates
chosen for its cells (left to right) and its dithered rows: the same
result as `ditherCells`. A band's rows are read and dithered only when
the band is first needed, so only one band is in memory. When a band
holds a row whose length differs from the first row's, `ditherBands`
stops there with an error naming it; the bands before it have come out.
declarations.title: ditherBands

modules.name: Puregrain.Cells

modules.comments:
Dithering a whole image, in three ways that give the same rows for the
same input, with a kernel (`Puregrain.Kernel`) and a quantizer
(`Puregrain.Quantize`, `Puregrain.Palette`, `Puregrain.Ordered`):

- `ditherImage`: an image in memory, all at once;
- `ditherRows`: a lazy stream of rows, each dithered when it's needed;
- `initDithering` and `ditherRow`: one row at a time, with you running
  the loop. For rows that come from effects, such as a network stream
  or a file read piece by piece:

```purescript
-- readRow and writeRow are your own, here in Aff
loop :: Dithering Number -> Aff Unit
loop dithering = readRow >>= case _ of
  Nothing -> pure unit
  Just row -> case ditherRow dithering row of
    Left problem -> throwError (error problem)
    Right { row: dithered, next } -> writeRow dithered *> loop next

main = launchAff_ (loop (initDithering floydSteinberg (threshold 128.0)))
```

`Aff` keeps such a loop from growing the stack, however long the
stream; in `Effect`, write it with `tailRecM`.

declarations.comments:

- `a`: the pixel type, `Number` for gray, `RGB` or `RGBA`; any type

- `Array (Array a)`: the image, rows top to bottom, each left to right,

Returns the dithered image, all at once. Stops with an error naming a

- `a`, `Kernel` and `Quantize a`: as for `ditherImage`.
- `LL.List (Array a)`: the rows, top to bottom, all of the same length;

Returns the dithered rows as a lazy list, the same rows as

declarations.comments:
An image being dithered one row at a time, for `ditherRow`: the

An immutable value: keep and reuse one, for an undo, say. Dithering a

declarations.comments:
The state before the first row, for `ditherRow`.

- `Kernel`: where each pixel's error goes; `noDiffusion` for nowhere.

Computes nothing yet; the first row fixes the image's width.

modules.name: Puregrain.Dither

modules.comments:
The queues that carry error fractions from the pixel that produces
them to the pixel that receives them, and their implementations.
Internal: may change without notice.

children.comments:
`replicate n x` builds a `Fifo` containing exactly `n` copies of
`x`, in order — so `dequeue` on the result yields `x` exactly `n`
times before the `Fifo` becomes empty.

Called once per row, to build the leading zero-padding for an
offset with a positive `dx` (see `Puregrain.Internal.Kernel.paddingFor`), and
to build the leading zero-padding for the `current`/`building`
layers at the start of every row. `n` is always small — bounded
by the kernel's horizontal reach (its largest `dx`), never by image
width or height.

Target complexity: O(n). Since `n` is always small, this is never
the bottleneck regardless of the instance's constant factors.
children.title: replicate

children.comments:
`enqueue fifo x` appends `x` to the tail of `fifo`, returning the
extended `Fifo`. `fifo` itself is left unchanged — anyone still
holding a reference to it must keep seeing the original,
unextended contents (this is a pure, persistent operation, not a
mutation).

Called exactly once per pixel, for every offset with `dy == 0`
(`current`) and every offset with `dy > 0` (`building`). This is
the single hottest operation in the whole algorithm: its `O(n)`
cost on `Data.List.Lazy` — where `n` grows up to the image width
over the course of a row — is exactly what produced the
`O(width²)`-per-row, `O(width³)`-per-square-image blowup recorded
in `docs/benchmarks-fifo.md`.

Target complexity: O(1) amortized. An instance that can only
offer O(n) here reintroduces precisely the bug this class exists
to fix.
children.title: enqueue

children.comments:
`dequeue fifo` removes and returns the value at the head of
`fifo`, together with the remaining `Fifo` — or `Nothing` if
`fifo` is empty.

Called exactly once per pixel, for every offset being read this
row (`current` and `matured`). Together with `enqueue`, this
bounds the per-pixel cost of the whole algorithm.

`Nothing` is a real, expected outcome only when padding runs out
at the very edge of the image. `Puregrain.Internal.Step` treats any other
`Nothing` as a violated invariant and crashes loudly rather than
silently substituting a value — instances must not paper over
emptiness themselves (e.g. by returning a fabricated zero).

Target complexity: O(1) amortized.
children.title: dequeue

children.comments:
`replace skip fifo` drops the first `skip` elements from the
front of `fifo` and appends `skip` zeros to the tail, returning a
`Fifo` of the SAME LENGTH as the input. `skip` is always small
(bounded by the kernel's horizontal reach — see
`Puregrain.Internal.Kernel.skipFor`), but `fifo` itself may be as long as the
image width by the time this is called.

Called once per row, per offset with a negative `dx`, in
`Puregrain.Internal.Row.commitBuilding` — this re-aligns a fully-built row's
worth of error fractions with the next row's pixel positions
before it's handed off to its `DelayLine` slot.

This is its own method — rather than being left for callers to
express as "drop, then append a small replicated tail" — because
that composition is O(n) on a plain singly-linked list even
though `skip` is small (the append has to walk and rebuild the
entire dropped-and-kept prefix). An instance backed by a
structure with cheap concatenation (e.g. a finger tree, where
append is O(log(min(n1, n2)))) should implement `replace` using
that capability directly, to actually realize the better
complexity — not by delegating to `drop` + `<>`.

Target complexity: better than O(n) where the underlying
structure allows it. O(n) is acceptable only if the instance
genuinely cannot do better, and should be called out as a known
limitation in that instance's own documentation.
children.title: replace

children.comments:
Sanity-check baseline instance: this is the representation the
project used before `class Fifo` existed. `enqueue` and `replace`
are both O(n) here (a plain singly-linked list has no cheap way to
append at the tail) — an instance of `Fifo` using this should
reproduce the `O(N³)` scaling recorded for square images in
`docs/benchmarks-fifo.md`, not improve on it. Kept around specifically
to verify that the abstraction itself introduces no regression
relative to the pre-`class Fifo` code, and as a point of comparison
for the `CatQueue` instance below.
children.title: <anonymous>

children.comments:
The production default (`Puregrain.Internal.Image.ditherImage`). It replaced
`Data.Sequence.Seq`, the finger tree that first fixed the O(N³)
scaling (docs/benchmarks-fifo.md), on 2026-10-03: about 3.6× faster,
and a registry package instead of a git fork
(docs/benchmarks-dithering.md).

`Data.CatQueue` (package `catenable-lists`) is Okasaki's strict
two-list queue: a front list to dequeue from and a back list,
newest first, to enqueue onto. `enqueue` (`snoc`) is O(1).
`dequeue` (`uncons`) is O(1) amortized: when the front list runs
out, it reverses the back list once, in O(n). `replace skip` is
`skip` dequeues followed by `skip` enqueues of `zero`, so O(skip)
amortized, and `skip` is at most the kernel's reach. `replicate`
builds straight into the front list, so a fresh queue never needs
reversing.

The amortized bounds hold only if each queue version is used once:
an old version used again would redo the same reversal. `step` and
`stepRow` use them that way, since every operation's result
replaces its input. Reusing a whole row's state (the public
`Dithering`) is fine: stepping from it again redoes that row's work,
the reversal included, and no more.
children.title: <anonymous>

declarations.comments:
A FIFO-like container of `Number`s, used to hold error-diffusion
fractions for a single kernel offset as they travel from the pixel
that produced them to the pixel that consumes them.

Every method below is called exactly once per pixel (or once per
row, where noted) in the dithering hot path, so the real-world
performance of the whole algorithm is dominated by how cheaply an
instance can implement these four operations. Each instance should
document its own actual complexity per method, and should aim for
the target given here wherever its underlying representation
allows it — falling short of the target is not a correctness bug,
but it will show up directly in `docs/benchmarks-fifo.md`.
declarations.title: Fifo

modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.Fifo

modules.comments:
The two drivers that run the diffusion over a whole image, row by row,
with any `Fifo` backend: `ditherImageWith` over an array of rows (all at
once) and `ditherRowsWith` over a lazy list of rows (each when asked
for). Both drive the same `stepRow`, so they give the same result; a
row of a different length, a `Left` from `stepRow`, becomes a runtime
error here, since neither result type can carry it.
Internal: `Puregrain.Dither` exports them with the production backend;
the tests use them to check every backend against a reference.

declarations.comments: An image in memory: a strict fold over the array of rows.
declarations.title: ditherImageWith

declarations.comments: A stream of rows: a lazy unfold over the list of rows.
declarations.title: ditherRowsWith

modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.Image

modules.comments:
The compiled form of a kernel, built once per image so the per-pixel
step doesn't filter the kernel again for every pixel (PureScript
shares nothing automatically). Internal: may change without notice.

declarations.comments:
Precomputed per kernel: the offsets in the current row, the offsets
of each later row grouped by `dy` (layer i holds those with
`dy == i + 1`), and the deepest `dy`. Built once by `compileKernel`,
then passed on as plain data through the row and step code.
declarations.title: CompiledKernel

modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.Kernel

modules.comments:
One row of the diffusion: the step for each pixel, then handing the
row's queues over to the rows below. Internal: may change without
notice.

declarations.comments:
Dithers one row and returns the state for the next one. States are
plain immutable values: stepping from an old one again (an undo, say)
redoes that row's work, the queues' list reversals included, and no
more.

Every row must be as long as the first one. A row of a different
length is a caller's bug: `Left` with a message naming the row,
rather than reading past the queued error or leaving it misaligned
for the rows below. The state isn't touched, so the caller can retry.
declarations.title: stepRow

declarations.comments:
The other half of `stepRow`'s contract: its `Left` (a row of a
different length, a caller's bug) becomes a stop with the same
message. For the drivers whose result type can't carry an error:
`ditherImage` and `ditherRows` (`Puregrain.Internal.Image`), and
`ditherCells` and `ditherBands` (`Puregrain.Cells`).
declarations.title: orStop

modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.Row

modules.comments:
The state the diffusion carries along: the queues of error fractions
waiting for later pixels. Internal: may change without notice.

declarations.comments:
One queue per kernel offset of one row: the error fractions on their
way to the pixels of a later row (or, for the current row's offsets,
to pixels further right).
declarations.title: RowLayer

declarations.comments:
The maturing `RowLayer`s for one `dy`. It starts padded with `dy`
copies of the empty `RowLayer` (`[]`): a placeholder that contributes
zero error for free (`sumErrors [] = zero`), with no special case in
the step. An `Array` rather than a queue: it's always short, at most
the kernel's `maxDepth`.
declarations.title: DelayLine

declarations.comments:
What crosses from one row to the next: the delay lines; the index of
the next row (`nextRow`, the `y` the quantizer will see), kept here
rather than passed in, so a caller stepping row by row can't pass a
wrong one; and the image's `width`, taken from the first row
(`Nothing` before it), which every later row must match.

A plain immutable value: stepping from an old state again (an undo,
say) redoes that row's work, the queues' list reversals included, and
no more (see the `CatQueue` instance in `Puregrain.Internal.Fifo`).
declarations.title: DitherState

declarations.comments:
Row-local state, rebuilt for every pixel. `x` is the column of the
next pixel and `y` this row's index — carried here rather than
computed by an indexed traversal, because `step` rebuilds this record
per pixel anyway (no extra allocation), whereas `mapAccumLWithIndex`
on Array is a generic default with an extra pass per row.
declarations.title: RowState

modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.State

modules.comments:
One pixel of the diffusion: add up the error arriving from earlier
pixels, quantize, and send the new error on to the queues.
Internal: may change without notice.
modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.Step

modules.comments: Small helpers. Internal: may change without notice.

declarations.comments:
Like `(..)`, but returns `[]` when `lo > hi` instead of PureScript's
native descending-range behaviour (`1 .. 0 == [1, 0]`, not `[]` —
unlike Haskell's `[1..0] == []`). This codebase always wants the
Haskell-like "empty when inverted" semantics: every call site
builds a range from 1 up to some count that is legitimately allowed
to be 0 (e.g. `maxDepth`), and expects zero elements in that case,
not a spurious 2-element descending array.
declarations.title: safeRange

modules.name: Puregrain.Internal.Util

modules.comments:
Error-diffusion kernels: where each pixel's quantization error goes,
and in what shares.

Use a ready-made kernel (`floydSteinberg`, `atkinson`,
`jarvisJudiceNinke`, or `noDiffusion` for none), or build your own
from a list of offsets with `fromOffsets`, which checks it.

declarations.comments:
One neighbour that gets a share of a pixel's error.

- `dx`: columns to the right; negative to the left.
- `dy`: rows down.
- `weight`: the share of the error.
declarations.title: Offset

declarations.comments:
A checked list of neighbours. Build one with `fromOffsets`, or use a
ready-made one. Opaque, so every kernel `ditherImage` gets is valid.
declarations.title: Kernel

declarations.comments:
Checks a list of offsets and makes it a kernel.

- `Array Offset`: the neighbours and their shares.

`Left` says which offset breaks which rule (offsets counted from 0):

- every offset must point to a pixel not yet processed, in row-by-row
  scan order: a later row (`dy > 0`), or the same row further right
  (`dy == 0`, `dx > 0`);
- every weight must be a finite number (not NaN or infinite);
- no two offsets may point to the same neighbour.

The weights usually add up to 1, but needn't: Atkinson's add up to
3/4 on purpose. An empty list is valid: it's `noDiffusion`.

```purescript
-- half of the error to the right, half down
fromOffsets [ { dx: 1, dy: 0, weight: 0.5 }, { dx: 0, dy: 1, weight: 0.5 } ]
```
declarations.title: fromOffsets

declarations.comments: The kernel's offsets, as given to `fromOffsets`.
declarations.title: offsets

declarations.comments: Floyd–Steinberg (1976): 4 neighbours, the classic.
declarations.title: floydSteinberg

declarations.comments:
Atkinson (Apple, 1980s): 6 neighbours over the next 2 rows, each
getting 1/8, so only 3/4 of the error is passed on: crisper and
higher in contrast, at the cost of detail in dark and light tones.
declarations.title: atkinson

declarations.comments:
Jarvis–Judice–Ninke (1976): 12 neighbours over the next 2 rows, for
the smoothest texture, at about 2.5 times Floyd–Steinberg's cost.
declarations.title: jarvisJudiceNinke
noDiffusion

modules.name: Puregrain.Kernel

modules.comments:
The ZX Spectrum's screen: 8 × 8 cells, each with two colors, an ink
and a paper, from the machine's 8 colors, plus one BRIGHT bit for both.
With `Puregrain.Cells`, that gives images the Spectrum could show:

```purescript
import Puregrain.Cells (ditherCells, nearestInCell, orderedInCell)
import Puregrain.Machine.ZxSpectrum as Zx

-- ordered dithering inside the cells, with a threshold map m
{ cells, image } = ditherCells noDiffusion (orderedInCell m) Zx.screen picture

-- error diffusion inside the cells
{ cells, image } = ditherCells atkinson nearestInCell Zx.screen picture
```

Ordered dithering, with the 8 × 8 Bayer map, looks most like the
Spectrum's own art and keeps every tone; with error diffusion,
Atkinson looks best.

`cells` holds each cell's `Attribute`: its ink, paper and BRIGHT, as a
screen file needs them; `toScr` turns the whole result into one. The
colors are those of `Puregrain.Palette.Presets.zxSpectrum`. The
colors, the attributes and the file layouts in full:
[docs/machine-screens/zx-spectrum.md](https://github.com/roman-mkh/puregrain/blob/master/docs/machine-screens/zx-spectrum.md).

declarations.comments:
One cell's attribute: its ink and paper, as ZX color codes (0 black,
1 blue, 2 red, 3 magenta, 4 green, 5 cyan, 6 yellow, 7 white), and
whether BRIGHT is set. Only the 71 values in `attributes` exist.
declarations.title: Attribute

declarations.comments: The ink's color code, 0 to 7.
declarations.title: ink

declarations.comments: The paper's color code, 0 to 7.
declarations.title: paper

declarations.comments: Whether BRIGHT is set, for both ink and paper.
declarations.title: bright

declarations.comments:
Every attribute that looks different: per brightness, 8 cells of a
single color and 28 pairs, 72 in all, minus one, because all black
looks the same with and without BRIGHT (it's listed once, without).
Ink is the darker color, the lower code, and paper the lighter, as in
the Spectrum's default of black ink on white paper; a single-color
cell has ink = paper.

They're listed in the order `Puregrain.Cells` tries them, where the
earlier wins a tie: the single colors first, then the pairs by the
distance between their two colors, nearest first (at equal distances,
normal before bright, then by ink, then by paper). A cell that several
palettes fit equally well thus gets the narrowest, the calmest.
declarations.title: attributes

declarations.comments:
The attribute's colors, for `Puregrain.Cells`: the ink, then the
paper, or the one color of a single-color cell. With `orderedInCell`,
the order means that a cell is ink with paper dots added as a pixel
nears the paper.
declarations.title: attributePalette

declarations.comments:
The Spectrum's screen mode, for `Puregrain.Cells`: cells of 8 × 8
pixels, each using one of the `attributes`, tried in their order, with
`attributePalette`'s colors.
declarations.title: screen

declarations.comments:
A dithered screen as a `.scr` file: the 6912 bytes of the Spectrum's
screen memory, as `SAVE "name" SCREEN$` saves them, and as many
emulators and tools open them.

- `{ cells, image }`: what `Puregrain.Cells.ditherCells` returns with
  this module's `screen`, for a 256 × 192 picture.

```purescript
bytes = toScr (ditherCells noDiffusion (orderedInCell m) screen picture)
```

The first 6144 bytes are the bitmap, one bit per pixel (1 for the ink,
0 for the paper, the leftmost pixel in the highest bit), its rows in the
Spectrum's interleaved order. Then come 768 attribute bytes, one per
cell, row by row: BRIGHT × 64 + paper × 8 + ink, with FLASH off. A
single-color cell has all its bits 0.

`Left`, with a message, for an image that isn't 256 × 192, for cells
that don't form the matching 32 × 24 grid, or for a pixel that isn't
one of its cell's colors: then the cells weren't chosen for this image.
declarations.title: toScr

declarations.comments:
A dithered screen as a `.tap` tape image: a short BASIC program that
starts by itself and loads the screen, then the screen as a CODE file.
Open it in an emulator, or type `LOAD ""` on a Spectrum: the picture
appears and stays until a key is pressed.

- `String`: the name on the tape, up to 10 printable ASCII characters.
- `{ cells, image }`: as for `toScr`.

```purescript
bytes = toTap "sphere" (ditherCells noDiffusion (orderedInCell m) screen picture)
```

`Left`, with a message, for a name that's too long or holds other
characters, and as `toScr` for the screen. The tape format:
https://worldofspectrum.net/zx-modules/fileformats/tapformat.html
declarations.title: toTap

modules.name: Puregrain.Machine.ZxSpectrum

modules.comments:
Ordered dithering: a quantizer whose decision between two
neighbouring levels depends on the pixel's position, through a
repeating grid of thresholds — a threshold map. The best known one is
the Bayer matrix (Bryce E. Bayer, Kodak, 1973).

It's an ordinary `Quantize`, so it works with `ditherImage` like any
other quantizer. With `noDiffusion` (no error passed on), that gives
pure ordered dithering; with any other kernel, the hybrid
"threshold modulation": error diffusion keeps the tones right, and
the map decides where the dots land. Background, formulas and what to
look for: [docs/ordered-dithering.md](https://github.com/roman-mkh/puregrain/blob/master/docs/ordered-dithering.md).

declarations.comments:
A threshold map: a grid of thresholds, each strictly between 0 and 1,
repeated across the image. Build one with `bayer` or
`compileThresholdMap`; opaque, so every map is checked: rectangular
and non-empty.
declarations.title: ThresholdMap

declarations.comments:
The Bayer threshold map.

- `Int`: the side, a power of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, …).

`Nothing` for any other side. The thresholds are `(rank + 0.5) / n²`
for side `n` (see `compileThresholdMap`). `bayer 1` is 0.5 everywhere:
`ordered` with it picks the nearer level, like `nearestLevel`.

```purescript
-- pure 1-bit ordered dithering with the 8 × 8 map
map (\m -> ditherImage noDiffusion (ordered m (evenRamp 2)) image) (bayer 8)
```
declarations.title: bayer

declarations.comments:
The ranks of a Bayer matrix: the order in which its cells turn on.

- `Int`: the side, a power of 2 (1, 2, 4, 8, …).

`Nothing` for any other side. Built by the standard recursion from the
1 × 1 matrix `[[0]]`:

```
M₂ₙ = | 4·Mₙ + 0   4·Mₙ + 2 |
      | 4·Mₙ + 3   4·Mₙ + 1 |
```

so `bayerMatrix 2 == Just [[0, 2], [3, 1]]`, and every rank from 0 to
n² − 1 appears exactly once. The result has n² entries: mind the size
for large `n`.
declarations.title: bayerMatrix

declarations.comments:
A threshold map from your own ranks: a clustered-dot screen or a
blue-noise mask, say.

- `Array (Array Int)`: the ranks, row by row: the order in which the
  cells turn on as the input rises. The grid needn't be square, and
  ranks may repeat or skip values.

Each cell's threshold is `(rank + 0.5) / (maxRank + 1)`, strictly
between 0 and 1. `Left` says what's wrong: no rows, an empty row, rows
of different lengths, or a negative rank (rows and columns counted
from 0).
declarations.title: compileThresholdMap

declarations.comments:
The threshold at a pixel's position; the map repeats across the image.

- `ThresholdMap`: the map.
- `{ x :: Int, y :: Int | r }`: the position, any record with `x` and
  `y`, such as a quantizer's `Context`.

Column `x` uses the map's column `x mod width`, row `y` its row
`y mod height`.
declarations.title: thresholdAt

declarations.comments:
Ordered dithering over levels. For a value `v` between two
neighbouring levels `lo` < `hi`, it picks `hi` exactly when
`(v − lo) / (hi − lo)` is above the pixel's threshold, else `lo`.

- `ThresholdMap`: the thresholds, from `bayer` or
  `compileThresholdMap`.
- `NonEmptyArray Number`: the levels, in any order; with 0 and 255,
  classic 1-bit ordered dithering.

A value at a level stays that level; values beyond the lowest or
highest level snap to it, as accumulated error can push them there in
the hybrid with error diffusion. For color, lift it with `perChannel`,
which gives every channel the same position.
declarations.title: ordered

modules.name: Puregrain.Ordered

modules.comments:
Dithering to a palette: each pixel becomes the nearest palette color,
with all three channels chosen together. `nearestColor` is the ready
quantizer; ready-made palettes (black and white, web-safe, CGA, ANSI,
Commodore 64, ZX Spectrum) are in `Puregrain.Palette.Presets`.

Distances are plain RGB distances, which aren't perceptual: pure green
is nearer to black than to white.

declarations.comments:
A palette ready to search: its colors, never empty, and the distance
to search them by. Build it once per image with `compilePalette` or
`compilePaletteFromArray`; read its colors with `paletteColors`.
Opaque, so its representation may change, to make the search faster,
say.
declarations.title: CompiledPalette

declarations.comments:
Makes a palette ready to search.

- `RGB -> RGB -> Number`: the distance between a pixel and a color,
  usually `distance2`.
- `NonEmptyArray RGB`: the colors.

```purescript
palette = compilePalette distance2 websafe216
```
declarations.title: compilePalette

declarations.comments:
As `compilePalette`, for colors in a plain `Array`, as they come from
JSON or JavaScript, say.

- `RGB -> RGB -> Number`: the distance, usually `distance2`.
- `Array RGB`: the colors.

`Nothing` for an empty array.
declarations.title: compilePaletteFromArray

declarations.comments: The palette's colors, in the order they were given.
declarations.title: paletteColors

declarations.comments:
The squared distance between two colors in RGB, the usual metric for
palettes: (r₁ − r₂)² + (g₁ − g₂)² + (b₁ − b₂)². Squared, since finding
the nearest color only compares distances.
declarations.title: distance2

declarations.comments:
The palette's color nearest to a pixel, by the palette's distance; on
a tie, the earlier color. For many pixels, compile the palette once;
`nearestColor` does that for you.

- `CompiledPalette`: the palette.
- `RGB`: the pixel.
declarations.title: nearestColorFast

declarations.comments:
A quantizer that turns each pixel into the nearest palette color, all
three channels together, by `distance2`; on a tie, the earlier color.

- `NonEmptyArray RGB`: the palette, e.g. from
  `Puregrain.Palette.Presets`.

```purescript
ditherImage floydSteinberg (nearestColor websafe216) image
```
declarations.title: nearestColor

modules.name: Puregrain.Palette

modules.comments:
Ready-made fixed palettes, for `Puregrain.Palette.nearestColor`.
Each is a plain `NonEmptyArray RGB`, not a `CompiledPalette`, so the
caller picks the distance metric: `compilePalette distance2 cga16`.

Historical and terminal palettes have no single official RGB
definition — machines were analog, terminals are themable — so each
preset below says where its values come from. Overview, sources and
notes: [docs/palettes.md](https://github.com/roman-mkh/puregrain/blob/master/docs/palettes.md).

Order matters in one respect: when a pixel is exactly as near to two
colors, `nearestColor` picks the one that comes first.

declarations.comments:
Black, then white. With `nearestColor` it dithers a color image
straight down to pure black and white, choosing by RGB distance —
which isn't brightness: pure green is nearer to black.
declarations.title: blackWhite

declarations.comments:
The 216 "web-safe" colors: every combination of 0, 51, 102, 153, 204
and 255 per channel (a 6×6×6 cube), `r` varying slowest, so it starts
at black and ends at white. Being a complete grid, its nearest color is
the nearest step in each channel separately — the same result as
`perChannel (nearestLevel (evenRamp 6))`.
declarations.title: websafe216

declarations.comments:
The 16-color IBM PC palette, CGA's "RGBI" colors in index order 0–15:
each channel 0x00 or 0xAA, plus an intensity bit adding 0x55, with the
IBM 5153 monitor's brown (color 6 is #AA5500, not dark yellow). Also
EGA's and VGA's defaults and the DOS text colors; the Linux console
uses the same values, in ANSI order. EGA's full 64 colors need no
preset: `perChannel (nearestLevel (evenRamp 4))`.
Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Color_Graphics_Adapter (RGBI palette).
declarations.title: cga16

declarations.comments:
The 16 ANSI terminal colors as xterm's defaults, in index order: black,
red, green, yellow, blue, magenta, cyan, white, then the 8 bright ones.
ANSI names the colors but defines no RGB, and terminals differ; the
Linux console's values are `cga16`, in CGA order.
Source: xterm's XTerm-col.ad, matching the xterm column of
en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ANSI_escape_code.
declarations.title: ansi16

declarations.comments:
xterm's 256 colors: `ansi16` (indices 0–15), a 6×6×6 cube (16–231,
index 16 + 36r + 6g + b, levels 0, 95, 135, 175, 215, 255), and 24
grays (232–255, 8 + 10i). 7 cube colors repeat `ansi16` ones, so 249
are distinct; `nearestColor` picks the earlier index of a pair. In a
real terminal the first 16 come from its theme.
Source: xterm's 256colres.pl.
declarations.title: ansi256

declarations.comments:
The Commodore 64's 16 colors, in VIC-II index order: black, white, red,
cyan, purple, green, blue, yellow, orange, brown, light red, dark grey,
grey, light green, light blue, light grey. There's no official RGB
definition; these are Pepto's calculated PAL values (2001, gamma
corrected), the de facto reference.
Source: pepto.de/projects/colorvic/2001/
declarations.title: c64

declarations.comments:
The ZX Spectrum's 15 distinct colors: its 8 (black, blue, red, magenta,
green, cyan, yellow, white) at normal brightness, then the 7 non-black
ones with BRIGHT (bright black is black). Normal is 0xD8 = 216, about
85% of bright, the common model: the real colors were never measured,
and many emulators use 0xD7 or 0xCD instead. This is the per-pixel
palette; for the real machine's 2 colors per 8×8 cell, see
`Puregrain.Machine.ZxSpectrum`.
Source: en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ZX_Spectrum_graphic_modes; values as
lospec.com/palette-list/zx-spectrum.
declarations.title: zxSpectrum

modules.name: Puregrain.Palette.Presets

modules.comments:
Pixel types: a single gray channel (`Gray`, a plain `Number`), `RGB`
and `RGBA`, with channel values on the 0–255 scale by convention.

Error diffusion adds and subtracts error, so a pixel type must be a
`Ring`, and `Scalable` by the kernel's `Number` weights. `MapChannels`
lets a one-channel quantizer work on every channel of a pixel (see
`Puregrain.Quantize.perChannel`).

declarations.comments:
A gray pixel: one channel, a plain `Number`, from 0 (black) to 255
(white) by convention.
declarations.title: Gray

children.comments: Compared and shown like the record inside.
children.title: <anonymous>

children.comments:
Channel by channel, `mul` and `one` too, though error diffusion uses
only `add`, `zero` and `sub`.
children.title: <anonymous>

declarations.comments:
A color pixel: red, green and blue, each from 0 to 255 by convention.
Adds, subtracts and scales channel by channel, as error diffusion
needs.
declarations.title: RGB

children.comments:
Alpha too, like the other channels, as in the `Ring` and `Scalable`
instances.
children.title: <anonymous>

declarations.comments:
A color pixel with alpha: as `RGB`, plus `a`, which error diffusion
treats like the other channels.
declarations.title: RGBA

children.comments:
Multiplies every channel by a weight.

- `Number`: the weight, a kernel's share of the error.
- `a`: the pixel.
children.title: scale

declarations.comments:
A pixel type that error diffusion can scale by a kernel's weights.
With `Ring`, for adding and subtracting error, it's what `ditherImage`
needs from a pixel type.
declarations.title: Scalable

children.comments:
Applies the function to every channel, independently.

- `Number -> Number`: the function for one channel.
- `a`: the pixel.
children.title: mapChannels

children.comments:
A gray pixel is its one channel: `perChannel` on `Number` is the
quantizer itself.
children.title: <anonymous>

children.comments:
Alpha too, like the other channels, as in the `Ring` and `Scalable`
instances.
children.title: <anonymous>

declarations.comments:
A pixel type whose channels can be mapped one by one: what
`Puregrain.Quantize.perChannel` needs to run a one-channel quantizer
on every channel. Laws, as for any functor-like mapping:

```purescript
mapChannels identity == identity
mapChannels (f <<< g) == mapChannels f <<< mapChannels g
```
declarations.title: MapChannels

modules.name: Puregrain.Pixel

modules.comments:
Quantizers: the step of dithering that picks an output value for each
pixel. A `Quantize a` gets the pixel's value, with the error diffused
into it already added, and the pixel's position; `ditherImage` diffuses
the difference between the two to the neighbours.

Ready-made: `threshold` (1-bit), `nearestLevel` with `evenRamp` (a few
levels), and `perChannel` to use either on every channel of a color
pixel. Palettes are in `Puregrain.Palette`, ordered (Bayer) dithering
in `Puregrain.Ordered`. Build your own with `quantize` (position-blind)
or `quantizeWith` (uses the position).

declarations.comments:
A quantizer: picks a pixel's output value; `a` is the pixel type.
Build one with `quantize`, or `quantizeWith` when the decision depends
on the pixel's position; run one with `runQuantize`. Opaque, so its
representation can change without breaking anyone.

It gets the pixel's corrected value, with the error diffused into it
already added, and must be total: accumulated error pushes values
beyond the nominal range, below 0 or above 255, and the quantizer must
still return a sensible value. `ditherImage` diffuses the difference
between the corrected value and the output to the neighbours.
declarations.title: Quantize

declarations.comments:
Where the pixel being quantized sits: column `x` and row `y`, from 0
at the top-left. A record so it can grow, with a seed say, without
breaking quantizers: a helper that needs only some fields can take
`forall r. { x :: Int, y :: Int | r }`.
declarations.title: Context

declarations.comments:
A quantizer that ignores the pixel's position, the common case.

- `a -> a`: from the corrected value to the output value.

```purescript
-- 1-bit with the cut at 100
quantize \v -> if v < 100.0 then 0.0 else 255.0
```
declarations.title: quantize

declarations.comments:
A quantizer that also gets the pixel's position: ordered or noise
dithering, say, or a lookup in per-pixel data such as a mask.

- `Context -> a -> a`: from the position and the corrected value to
  the output value.

```purescript
-- 1-bit with the cut at 64 and 192 in a checkerboard
quantizeWith \{ x, y } v ->
  if v < (if (x + y) `mod` 2 == 0 then 64.0 else 192.0) then 0.0 else 255.0
```
declarations.title: quantizeWith

declarations.comments:
Runs a quantizer.

- `Quantize a`: the quantizer.
- `Context`: the pixel's position.
- `a`: the corrected value.

Returns the output value.
declarations.title: runQuantize

declarations.comments:
Runs a one-channel quantizer on every channel of a pixel,
independently, each with the pixel's position.

- `a`: the pixel type, with `MapChannels`: `Number`, `RGB` or `RGBA`.
- `Quantize Number`: the quantizer for one channel.

Dithering an RGB image this way gives exactly what dithering its three
channel planes separately would: a `Quantize Number` only ever sees
one channel, so it can't couple them. For a quantizer that looks at
the whole pixel, see `Puregrain.Palette.nearestColor`.

```purescript
-- 4 levels per channel
perChannel (nearestLevel (evenRamp 4)) :: Quantize RGB
```
declarations.title: perChannel

declarations.comments:
The classic 1-bit quantizer: 0 (black) below the threshold, 255
(white) at or above it.

- `Number`: the threshold, usually 128.

`nearestLevel (evenRamp 2)` is the same with the cut fixed at 127.5.
declarations.title: threshold

declarations.comments:
Snaps a value to the nearest of the given levels: the one-channel
sibling of `Puregrain.Palette.nearestColor`.

- `NonEmptyArray Number`: the levels, in any order; on an exact tie,
  the earlier wins.

Values below the lowest level snap to it, values above the highest to
that one.

```purescript
nearestLevel (evenRamp 4)   -- 0, 85, 170 or 255
```
declarations.title: nearestLevel

declarations.comments:
Evenly spaced levels from 0 to 255, both ends included, for
`nearestLevel`.

- `Int`: how many; 1 or less gives the single midpoint, 127.5.

`evenRamp 2 == [0.0, 255.0]`, `evenRamp 4 == [0.0, 85.0, 170.0, 255.0]`.
declarations.title: evenRamp

modules.name: Puregrain.Quantize

packageMeta.description: Error-diffusion and ordered (Bayer) dithering for PureScript: Floyd-Steinberg, Atkinson, JJN and custom kernels, retro palettes; in memory, streaming or row by row.
